entries.title: Bertie the Brain
entries.subtitle: An engineer gives the public an opponent
entries.summary: Josef Kates used a familiar game to introduce an unfamiliar machine at the Canadian National Exhibition.
body: In Toronto in 1950, visitors could challenge a machine at tic-tac-toe. Josef Kates built Bertie the Brain for the Canadian National Exhibition, using a keypad for the player's moves and a large illuminated display to show the contest. Its adjustable difficulty let the same installation offer different levels of resistance.

Kates was also demonstrating his Additron tube, an electronic component he had developed. A game gave that engineering a public face: instead of asking visitors to understand a circuit, Bertie asked them to make a move. The component did not become a commercial successor to conventional vacuum tubes, but the demonstration remains an early example of a computer opponent presented to ordinary visitors.

Bertie used lamps rather than a video screen. That distinction matters when comparing it with later experiments. It belongs in the origins of electronic play without needing to win a single, universal contest for the title of first video game.

entries.factual_note: The year and machine description are supported by Canada's History. The original flyer is linked as an artifact, not reproduced. No global first-video-game claim is made. Images still require a rights-cleared selection.

entries.title: OXO
entries.subtitle: A telephone dial becomes a game controller
entries.summary: Sandy Douglas put noughts and crosses on EDSAC, making a familiar contest part of life inside a computing laboratory.
body: Alexander 'Sandy' Douglas was a Cambridge PhD student when he made a noughts-and-crosses program for EDSAC, usually dated to 1952. The player entered moves with a rotary telephone dial. A small cathode-ray display showed the board, and the player could choose whether to move first or let the machine begin.

The setting shaped the audience. EDSAC was a research computer, so this was not a product that people could buy and take home. Few people outside Cambridge encountered the program. Its significance lies partly in that small scale: a laboratory machine could become something a person played against, with an input device, a visible position and a response to each decision.

The surviving EDSAC simulator and its documentation make that interaction approachable today. They also remind us to distinguish an original program from a later reconstruction. OXO is an important early graphical computer game; its position among other beginnings depends on whether we mean a stored program, an electronic display, moving images or public access.

sources.title: Alexander Douglas writes OXO for EDSAC
A Tutorial Guide to the EDSAC Simulator
sources.publisher: Martin Campbell-Kelly; EDSAC Replica Project, The National Museum of Computing

entries.factual_note: The simulator guide describes the program as developed about 1952; the year is conventional, not an exact day. Few outside Cambridge played it. Do not call Douglas's entire thesis a video-game thesis or imply a direct commercial lineage. Images still require a rights-cleared selection.
